was a global, calendar-driven bug with a known trigger date; correlated failures in a service network are typically probabilistic and triggered by environmental shocks with unknown timing.","Y2K could be detected and patched globally because the cause was known in advance; in a decentralized service network the shared cause is often discovered only post-failure.","The monolith with strict redundancy has no clean analog in Y2K; the analogy chiefly illustrates the hidden-coupling problem, not the relative resilience of a large redundant system."],"overturn_conditions":["Empirical audits showing decentralized nodes have fewer shared upstream dependencies (by count or criticality) than monoliths of equivalent capacity.","Evidence that large monolithic services exhibit the same or worse hidden-coupling risk (e.g., all internal replicas share one config daemon whose bugs are the dominant failure mode).","A theoretical proof that heterogeneity of small-service operators strictly bounds common-mode coupling to a small fraction of the network."],"shared_structure":["Y2K bug / epochal time rollover: many independently operated systems fail simultaneously because they share a hidden common dependency (calendar encoding) that is invisible until a common-mode trigger fires.","In both the small-services network and the Y2K case, apparent independence collapses into correlated failure when the shared latent cause is revealed."],"source_memory_refs":["local","background"],"transfer_claims":["The history of Y2K-like common-mode failures suggests that the visibility of shared dependencies, not the count of independent nodes, dominates correlated-failure risk.","This implies decentralized networks may appear safe but harbor correlated risks that surface only under rare external triggers, undercutting the resilience claim."]},"claim":"A decentralized network of small services is more fragile, not more resilient, under correlated failure than a monolithic service with strictly greater total internal redundancy, because the monolith can enforce homogeneous fault domains while the distributed nodes are exposed to common-mode external shocks whose coupling is hidden by decentralization until triggered.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the small services are air-gapped from one another's supply chains and infrastructure vendors, the argument fails and the distributed network is more resilient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service's internal redundancy shares a single common control plane (e.g., one orchestration daemon, one deployment config, one auth service) whose own bugs are the dominant correlated risk, then the monolith's redundancy is illusory and the distributed network becomes more resilient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If evidence shows small nodes have at least as much slack per unit capacity as the monolith (e.g., overprovisioned boxes in independent datacenters with no shared dependencies), the mechanism inverts and the distributed network is more resilient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Decentralization scatters nodes across heterogeneous environments whose true coupling (shared supply chain, energy grid, upstream cloud region, time-synchronized leap-second bug, common DNS provider, or epochal Y2K38 rollover) is not observable during normal operation; only the monolith's sheer internal redundancy (multi-AZ replication, excess disks, hot standby generators) absorbs a non-catastrophic shared shock. The small nodes lack internal slack, so the same external shock that the monolith survives wipes the network out at the first shared dependency, which is the dominant failure mode.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
